draft.title: Validity, sampling and bias
card: A valid investigation tests what it sets out to test. If the results could be caused by something other than the independent variable, the investigation is not valid.
To keep it valid, control the variables other than the one you change. Keep them the same in every trial so that only the independent variable can affect the result.
A sample is the group you actually test. A larger sample is less likely to be changed by a few unusual individuals, so its results are more trustworthy.
Bias is when how samples or observations are chosen favours one result. Choosing samples at random, and measuring in the same way each time, helps avoid it.
draft.remember: Valid means controlled variables, a large enough sample and no bias.

a.q: Why does a student control the variables other than the independent variable in an investigation?
opts: So that only the independent variable can affect the result
So that the results will always match the hypothesis
So that the sample can be made smaller
So that the results will be exactly the same each trial
a.why: Controlling the other variables means a change in the result can be linked to the independent variable, which makes the test valid. It does not make results match a hypothesis, because the test is still fair if the hypothesis is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what else could change the result.

b.q: Ravi tests whether a new fertiliser helps bean plants grow taller. He gives the fertiliser to the 5 healthiest-looking plants and no fertiliser to 5 weaker-looking plants. What is the main problem with his investigation?
opts: Bias in how he chose which plants got the fertiliser
The sample is too large to measure properly
He changed the amount of water given to both groups
He measured the height of the plants after growth
b.why: Choosing the healthiest plants for the fertiliser favours one result, so the difference could be due to plant health and not the fertiliser. Sorting the plants into groups at random would avoid this bias. Measuring plant height is a sensible way to see growth, so it is not the problem.
b.clue: Look at how the plants were put into the two groups.

a.best: So that only the independent variable can affect the result

b.best: Bias in how he chose which plants got the fertiliser

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the only one that is a noun phrase naming a card term ('Bias in how he chose…'), while the other three are 'He…' or 'The sample…' statements. Two of the distractors (measuring height after growth, a sample that is too large) are plainly not problems. A student could pick the answer by spotting the keyword 'Bias' without understanding the idea.

So that the sample can be made smaller
So that the results will be exactly the same each trial

b.q: Ravi has 60 bean plants in the same soil, light and water. He gives fertiliser to the 30 healthiest-looking plants and none to the other 30. After four weeks he measures every plant with the same ruler. Why might his results not be valid?
opts: Plant health, not fertiliser, could explain the results
Water, not fertiliser, could explain the results
The ruler used could favour the fertilised plants
There is no control group to compare the results with
b.why: Ravi chose the healthiest plants for the fertiliser, which is bias: they might grow taller anyway, so plant health could explain the results. Water is the same for every plant, so it is controlled. The 30 plants with no fertiliser are a group to compare with, and one ruler used the same way on every plant does not favour either group.
b.clue: Were the two groups alike before the test began?

a.best: So that only the independent variable can affect the result

b.best: Plant health, not fertiliser, could explain the results
